title: A Young Man Finally Speaks Up
overview: After Job has finished speaking and his three friends fall silent with no answer left, a younger listener named Elihu steps forward, angry at all of them, and explains why he now has to speak.

parts.label: Elihu enters, angry (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The three friends stop replying because they think Job is too sure of his own innocence, and Elihu, whose family names echo relatives of Abraham, has been listening the whole time. He is angry at Job for defending himself more than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without being able to answer him.

parts.label: Wisdom is not just age (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Custom gave older men the right to speak first, so Elihu held back out of respect. Now he argues that real understanding comes from the breath or spirit God puts in a person, not simply from years lived.

parts.label: The friends have failed (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: Elihu says he followed every argument closely, and none of them actually answered Job. He warns them not to excuse themselves by saying only God can deal with Job, and he promises to argue differently than they did.

parts.label: Ready to burst (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: He describes the friends as stunned into silence, while he is like new wine fermenting in a goatskin with no vent, about to split. He says he must speak just to get relief.

parts.label: No flattery (vv. 21-22)
parts.note: Elihu vows not to take sides or flatter anyone, likely echoing Job's earlier charge that the friends were biased in God's favor. He says God would soon take him away if he did.

disagreement: Interpreters differ over whether Elihu brings genuine insight that prepares the way for God's own speech, or is another overconfident voice whose long buildup the book presents with some irony.
think: When someone with less experience or standing challenges people who have more, what makes you willing to take their view seriously?
